text: It would be easy to read the last two lessons and conclude SOAR is heading toward replacing the analyst role entirely. It isn't. SOAR is a force multiplier: it removes the repetitive, well-understood portion of the workload so the same team can handle a far higher alert volume -- but every playbook only covers scenarios someone already fully worked out in advance. Everything outside that stays a human's job.

A few categories make that concrete. A novel attack pattern has no pre-built playbook branch, because nobody has written the correct response to something that's never happened before. An ambiguous alert -- a VP logging in from an unusual location at 2 a.m. -- could be a compromise or an executive on a red-eye flight; a tool can see the login, but it can't know the travel itinerary or the deal being closed.

Even a well-built playbook occasionally hits a case it wasn't designed for, and someone has to recognize that the automated path doesn't apply. And every playbook that exists at all started as a human decision about what the correct response should be -- someone designs that logic, tests it before trusting it with automated action, and keeps revising it as new attack patterns show up, the same tuning discipline correlation rules needed back in Chapter 3.

Some actions also carry consequences serious enough -- cutting an employee's access, a disclosure with legal implications -- that an organization keeps a human sign-off step even when the technical decision could be automated. That's a deliberate choice about accountability, not a gap in what SOAR is technically capable of.

Put together, SOAR doesn't shrink the analyst's role -- it changes what fills most of the day. Less time re-running the same lookup on report after report, more time on the investigations that actually require judgment. That's the force-multiplier relationship in practice, and the next lesson walks a full worked playbook end to end to show exactly where that human judgment still fits in.
